   U.S. farmers are increasingly utilizing drones to spray their farmland, says the American Farm Bureau Federation in a note. The AFBF says that 16.4 million acres of farmland were sprayed by drones in 2025, up roughly five times from 3.7 million acres in 2023. The usage of drones is increasing as farmers see them as ways to handle problems with accessing certain portions of their fields. “The biggest advantages for drones come in wet fields, rough terrain, irregularly shaped fields and situations where timely product applications are critical,” says Bernt Nelson of the AFBF. Drone usage in 2025 jumped 59% from 2024, the AFBF says. This year, excessive rainfall in many parts of the Corn Belt are making access to fields by combines harder to manage. (Kirk Maltais, kirk.maltais@wsj.com)

   It’s an open question as to which quantum computing company is positioned to lead a market expected to reach $10 billion in 2030, Morgan Stanley analysts write in a note. If fault-tolerant quantum computers become widely commercially adopted, that market could grow to $100 billion by 2040, they project. Still, everything hinges on technical execution and timing: each quantum company in Morgan Stanley’s coverage has a milestone set for 2027, with fault-tolerant systems expected in 2029 or 2030 per company roadmaps. “Today’s revenue is too small to show which businesses will succeed,” the analysts write. “The investment question is which companies are most likely to reach fault tolerance first.” (Elias Schisgall, elias.schisgall@wsj.com)

Plus, HSA tax benefits and a year of museum heists
 
 
ALEX NABAUM FOR WSJ
 

ETFs are cheap, but they aren’t cheap enough.

 

Exchange-traded funds have made owning swaths of stocks and bonds remarkably affordable. But if you move even slightly away from the broadest indexes like the S&P 500 or the aggregate U.S. bond market, ETFs often cost more than they should.

 

Below, some of the best analysis and insight from WSJ writers and columnists, the Dow Jones Newswires team and occasionally beyond, on investing, the wealth-management business and more.

Market Talk

 

From Dow Jones Newswires

 

U.S. farmers are increasingly utilizing drones to spray their farmland, says the American Farm Bureau Federation in a note. The AFBF says that 16.4 million acres of farmland were sprayed by drones in 2025, up roughly five times from 3.7 million acres in 2023. The usage of drones is increasing as farmers see them as ways to handle problems with accessing certain portions of their fields. “The biggest advantages for drones come in wet fields, rough terrain, irregularly shaped fields and situations where timely product applications are critical,” says Bernt Nelson of the AFBF. Drone usage in 2025 jumped 59% from 2024, the AFBF says. This year, excessive rainfall in many parts of the Corn Belt are making access to fields by combines harder to manage. (Kirk Maltais, kirk.maltais@wsj.com)

 

It’s an open question as to which quantum computing company is positioned to lead a market expected to reach $10 billion in 2030, Morgan Stanley analysts write in a note. If fault-tolerant quantum computers become widely commercially adopted, that market could grow to $100 billion by 2040, they project. Still, everything hinges on technical execution and timing: each quantum company in Morgan Stanley’s coverage has a milestone set for 2027, with fault-tolerant systems expected in 2029 or 2030 per company roadmaps. “Today’s revenue is too small to show which businesses will succeed,” the analysts write. “The investment question is which companies are most likely to reach fault tolerance first.” (Elias Schisgall, elias.schisgall@wsj.com)
